Can You Replace Your Desktop PC With a Raspberry Pi 4?
Why would anyone chose some stupid crap like that over a Desktop PC?

Let's see, the short answer is no. I'm a coder. (Embedded and graphics)

However my git server and media centre both run on two separate PI's and are doing very well.

I also supply PI's to external testers with parts of a system that need testing installed.

Yes I do have a few PI's laying around.

I am now looking at a webserver on yet another PI.

Is there any particular reason you go with a Pi vs a refurb desktop/laptop?

I have a few Pis (3s and 4s)as well, but in terms of performance, a $100 refurb is 10x the computer the Pi is out of the box.

I see a Pi system replacing a tablet in terms of ability, but stilling needing the desktop accessories - almost the worst of both worlds. That is why they sit on a shelf.

I have been looking at the refurb USFF pcs as well - I saw an I7/16GB version for $300ish. That was very tempting to me.

Keep in mind that I build embedded systems for a living. Originally the PI's were the most cost effective starting point for controllers.. So over time I developed a liking and a supply of the devices, as well as code library.

For me size is the biggest issue followed by price. There is enough grunt in a PI for most systems I build.

Keyboards, mice, screens are not usually needed so they're not an issue. The git server only has an ethernet connection.

So looking around at the moment I have two desktops running various flavours of Linux, 5 Pi's with various systems on them, And One very stock standard note book running out of the box windows for testing purposes.

I started running a PI as a terminal server ages ago and it was as you suggested ok but not great. This was when USB connections were shitty.

I have some older notebooks running linux when I needed a bit more grunt than a Pi.

I also have a fistful of older beagle boards, panda boards, and other's that I don't member the names, Including some Older X86 supposedly embedded boards where the x86 CPU needs a bloody fan. ( I think they still work)

I think PI's are really good for off loading CPU but originally not for desktop's. This may be different with the PI 4 B's but I don't have the incentive or time to see.

For embedded use, the Pi has pretty much every system beat.

I am using microchip for my work, with a few arduinos, but the "compiler to chip" step that can be avoided by using python on the Pi is very attractive. The biggest obstacle I have to going to Pi for everything is no onboard ADC. When an arduino has 6 analog inputs, and a pic has essentially all but 2-4 pins set as ADC inputs with up to 4 controllers, that built in functionality keeps the Pi out of projects.

Oh I should have mentioned, I also design hardware so adding interface chips of any sort as an addon board is not an issue for me.

So I agree that a straight PI is not that great for most embedded projects but adding additional hardware to a Pi is so damn easy.

Yeah, don't install your box in direct sunlight and don't install it on metal that is in direct sunlight.

Most of the problems with heat can be fixed with good airflow ( not necessarily with fans).

Heating issues mostly come up when your dealing with with environmentally protected enclosures. ( Level 3 for liquids and level 5 for dust. ) Up until these levels its common sense placement or a maintenance regime.

The higher levels of environmentally protected enclosures are difficult and thus require the big bucks. Some solutions are elegant and some are pretty brute force. It's really comes down to what the customer will pay for.

One design that got me was a device that used a mostly metal case for heat dissipation. The customer re purposed it for use on an animal. I got yelled at because the device burnt the animal. Originally it was to be used in water, but adding it to the collar on an animal meant heat dissipation dropped way down and it was also exposed to direct sunlight.

My projects would be in the 50-70C ambient temps on one end, and potentially the -40 on the other. I am not as worried with the cold, because I think the radiated heat of the Pi itself would help to keep everything warm, but when running at 70C ambient, I am worried that some of the components would fail.

Yeah but you probably want to add a back up. Dew point is the big killer at low temperatures. A simple transistor,/thermister feeding a current through a law value resistor is a cheap way to handle this, Note It won't be real accurate and watch out for the wattage rating of the resistor.
